Bill (No. 252). to amend the Act relating to Ocean Steamship subsidies.-(The Minister of Trade and Commerce) read the resolution, and House went into committee thereon.
If my memory serves me well, when we discussed this subject on a previous occasion the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) promised to give us information as to the status of the parties.	.
That information was placed oh the Table more than a week ago.
Would the right hon. gentleman please explain the scheme generally.

In 189C, the last year of the late government, a law was passed providing a subsidy for a direct line of navigation between France and Canada, the amount of the subsidy being $50,000. In 1901, this subsidy was increased, if I remember well to $100,000 for twenty-four trips. It so happens, unfortunately, that we have not been able to arrange for this line for the money voted. This year, we have made a contract with a Mr. Gustave Colombier, of Bordeaux, who has been recommended to us by the British consul at Bordeaux.
The terms of the contract are, in a few words, that this company binds itself to establish a line of steamers between Canada and France, to be provided with all modern apparatus, cold storage, &c. The tonnage will be 4,000 tons gross. The steamers will complete eighteen trips between Canada and France. It is provided that two of the steamers are to bear the French ting and two the British flag, but all the officers are to be British subjects.
What is the speed?
The speed will be about 12 knots.

I have heard that there are other persons connected with Mr. Co-lombier, either directly or indirectly. I would ask the Prime Minister whether Mr. Carbonneau has. either directly or indirectly, any connection with this transaction ? I have heard that that gentleman is, in some way, interested, either as a negotiator, or as a party, and I would like to know from the right horn, gentleman whether Mr. Carbonneau is a party in any shape to this contract.

So far as the government is concerned, Mr. Carbonneau is not a party to the contract in any shape whatever. Mr. Carbonneau has asked to be authorized to transfer bis contract to a company that he proposes to organize. We have answered that we will consider the transfer, if the terms are agreeable to us.

I understood the right hon. Prime Minister the other night to say that he had made inquiries about Mr. Co-lombier and bad received very satisfactory assurances with regard to that gentleman, I know nothing to the contrary, and I have no doubt that the information received by the right hon. gentleman is quite satisfactory so far as it relates to Mr. Colombier. But I have heard-it may be one of those rumours that people ought not to trust too far-that there are other people who are connected, or who pretend to be connected, with this transaction. I have heard that Mr. Carbonneau, whose name is not unknown in Canada, claims to have some interest in this matter as a negotiator, or to be in some shape directly or Indirectly connected with the contract. I would like the right lion, gentleman to tell us whether, not only in so far as the government is directly concerned but in any shape whatever, to his knowledge, Mr. Carbonneau lias had any interest or any part in this transaction or is in any way, connected with the negotiations or the contract.

I can only repeat what I have said-that, so far as the government is concerned we have had no communication whatever with Mr. Carbonneau. All our communications and negotiations have been with Mr. Colombier

alone, and Mr. Carbonneau has had nothing to do with the government directly or indirectly. I have heard that Mr. Carbonneau pretends that he is interested with Mr. Colombier. That has not come to me directly, but only as a rumour, it may be true or not true. At present, he has nothing to do with the contract-absolutely nothing. If Mr. Colombier assigns his contract to a company, as he may try to do, the name of Mr. Carbonneau may come before us then ; I do not know. We shall have to judge of the personnel of the company when it comes before us. But, at the present time, I beg to say in the most emphatic manner, we have absolutely nothing to do with Mr. Carbonneau.
Have any communications passed, since this matter was last before us, between the government and the Canadian agent general in France, Mr. Fabre ?
No.
Has Mr. Fabre been communicated with ?
No.

Mr. Fabre resides in Paris and for many years has been the representative of Canada in the capital of France. Is it not rather singular that, in a matter of so much importance to both countries, our agent general in France has not been communicated with and information aslced for from him as to the status of the gentleman entering into these negotiations ?

No, I think we have sought information from a gentleman who is better able to inform us as to the standing of the firm of Colombier than Mr. Fabre is. The British consul at Bordeaux is in a better position to give information as to character and standing of the firm of Colombier, and we sought information from him.

The right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has been good enough to place a paper in my hands the substance of which he communicated to the House some days ago. I recollect what was said then and so far as that is concerned, it seemed to me entirely satisfactory with regard to Mr. Colombier. The information was of that confidential character that I think would be quite satisfactory to the right hon. gentleman, and I have no hesitation in accepting it. But the question I am raising is somewhat apart from that. It is rumoured, and I understand the right hon. gentleman to say that he has heard the rumour, that Mr. Carbonneau claims to be in some way connected with this transaction, either concerned with Mr. Colombier, or in some way as negotiator, or interested in negotiations, with regard to the proposed contract. I am drawing attention to the
possibility that Mr. Carbonneau may be connected with this transaction. I do not say he is. The right hon. gentleman also has heard that he pretends to be connected with it, and all I desire to say at the present moment is that if I were in the position of the right hon. gentleman-though I never hope to be there-I would consider it my duty, knowing what I do of the reputation of Mr. Carbonneau, and hearing that he had some connection with this transaction,
I say I would consider it my duty to probe to the bottom that rumour, and if I found that he was connected with it, I would have great hesitation in entering into the bargain.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) is a little hypercritical in this matter. We have made a contract with Mr. Colombier, and my hon. friend is satisfied with the standing of Mr. Colombier. We have no relations with anybody else than Mr. Colombier. He has asked us if he could transfer his contract, saying that he wanted to organize a company, and we have given our consent, provided he submitted the personnel to us and we were satisfied with the conditions of the transfer. If, when Mr. Colombier makes application, we find that there are in this company parties who do not offer all the guarantees that the Canadian public and government have a right to expect, then it will be time to look into the matter more carefully. But as long as the affair remains as it is at present, when our negotiations are entirely with Mr. Colombier, I do not think we can do more than we have done, and I think my hon. friend will be disposed to agree with me.

I do not quite agree with the right hon. gentleman. If the right hon. gentleman, on behalf of the Dominion of Canada, is entering into this important con-| tract with Mr. Colombier, I submit, with all respect to the right hon. gentleman, that it is not sufficient for him to know the character of Mr. Colombier alone. If the right hon. gentleman has learned that there is even a suspicion that there are people connected with Mr. Colombier with whom the right hon. gentleman would not, on behalf of Canada, enter into a contract-and from what I have learned I think the right hon. gentleman would not enter into a contract with Mr. Carbonneau-if he has the slightest suspicion or reason to suspect that Mr. Carbonneau may be directly or indirectly connected with this transaction, although his name may never appear in the contract, and although the name of the gentleman who does appear in the contract may be as respectable as any man in this Dominion, I say I consider it the duty of the right hon. gentleman not to be content with the name of the man whose name appears in the contract, but to ascertain whether Mr. Car-

bonneau, or any other person who might be objectionable, is secretly a partner or in any way connected with Mr. Colombier in the contract. The right hon. gentleman says that when he comes to enter into this contract it will be time enough to inquire who are connected with it. I understand the contract is already entered into, and is before the House for confirmation. Conceding that the contract as it stands is with Mi-. Colombier alone, I ask, and I press, tlie right hon. gentleman to say, whether there is any reason to believe that there is anybody behind Mr. Colombier or connected with him in this transaction directly or indirectly, bearing the character which, I understand, Mr. Carbonneau bears.

There is no reason to believe that, so far as I have information-and I would not take idle rumour on the street to be any foundation-our relations have been with Mr. Colombier, whom we have found to be a perfect gentleman, and I think is of good commercial standing. He has told us that he is able to carry out the undertaking himself, with his own resources and those of his friends.
Is he carrying on) this contract himself or is he passing it over to another company ?
He intends to organize a company, but he will not be allowed to assign his contract to that company until he submits it to us for confirmation.
There was a cable from a gentleman signing himself ' Macdonald,' I presume he is the British consul. Is the copy of the cable sent to Mr. Macdonald forthcoming ? This is only his reply.

I have not been able to find the cable sent to him. The cable was sent by myself or by my secretary. My secretary has not been able to lay his hand upon it. The inquiry was as to the standing of Mr. Colombier.
Of course the telegraph company can supply copies of the cable.
If the hon. gentleman wants it he can get it before the third reading.

Apart from the personal considerations in a matter of so much importance as this, I think it is very esseiu-tial that we should not run any risks of making any more failures in our ocean steamship service. Before we enter into this contract the government should assure themselves that there is no risk of failure. We are just now entering upon a new course, we are opening up communication with France, a very wealthy country, whose people are very careful in entering int'o business operations of this kind, and they Mr. BARKER. .
would be adversely influenced in the event of a failure, either from the improper personnel of the Company undertaking the transaction or from want of business foresight on the part of the government. It may look to be a small matter, but I think in making an arrangement of this kind we should be very careful about the personnel of those with whom we are dealing. I myself have heard some rather adverse criticisms of the gentleman whose name is mentioned, not of the gentleman whose name appears as the contractor. I think it would be well, as suggested by my hon. friend from Hamilton, that the Prime Minister should have this matter thoroughly probed before he enters into the contract. Therefore, as these rumours have got abroad, not only in Montreal but they have also reached Ontario, that there is some influence at work in connection. with the transaction which would probably be detrimental to the high standing and character that the government of this country have at the present time, it behooves the government to proceed with a greater caution.

I was not in the House when this discussion began, and personally I know nothing about the gentlemen who are referred to. About a week or ten days ago I was in New York, and in one of the hotels I met by chance several gentlemen who happened to be talking about, this subsidy which was being obtained from the government for a line running between Canada and France. The statements that were made there in reference to some of the gentlemen connected with this scheme were so startling that I asked them if they could procure me any information on the subject. I received two days ago a mass of papers and statements. They are merely statements, and included amongst the papers is a copy of the ' British Columbia Review.' One of the gentlemen writes to me :
Dear Mr. Osier, I know nothing of the facts stated in this memorandum, but, if true they would seem to be matters of public importance.
I do not wish to read these statements, but I would like to hand them to the right hon. Prime Minister so that he can see what they are worth. I happened merely by chance to meet some gentlemen in New York, and during the course of the conversation which took place, one of them said :
' Canada seems to be the softest place to exploit that there is in the world to-day.' I do not wish to read these statements in the House, but I think it would be worth the while of the right hon. Prime Minister to look into them and see if there is anything in them at all. I simply state how I received them. I know nothing about them and as I stated, it was purely by accident that I came to know anything about the matter at all.
