We are discussing a question that is really outside of the resolution when we are discussing the propriety of organizing the territories into provinces. That is not the point in the resolution, and I think we-had better defer that question.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: We have proceeded so far upon that subject that it would he interesting to hear from the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) wliat has induced him to change his opinion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: The member for West Assiniboia has expressed no changed opinion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: I think when the discussion has reached this point and when certain statements have been made

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: There will he another opportunity for discussing the question of provincial autonomy. That is not in the resolution.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) desires to discuss the resolution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: If he intends to discuss the propriety of giving $250,000 to the North-west Territories, and confines himself to that, he will be perfectly in order.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext:
I merely wish to answer a couple of questions that have been brought to the attention of the House by the prem-

1232S
ier, but as you have decided that I am out of order, I will take another opportunity.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman goes on and makes another speech, then another hon. member will want to answer him, and I think we had better stop here. Carried.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: I desire to discuss the resolution. But before doing so, I wish to enter a protest against the chairman continually calling ' carried ' without putting the motion. I think it is proper that the members of the House should in every instance have a timely intimation that the chairman is going to put the question, by asking the committee plainly whether they are in favour of this resolution or not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is out of order. He rose to say he was going to speak to the resolution, and he is actually speaking to the chairman. In submitting motions in committee, I say ' Is this carried ' ? I do not say 1 Carried ' but 1 Is it carried.'

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: Well, the only word we have heard is ' carried.' However, I am going to deal with the resolution. I think we are making a mistake in creating a debt against the territories before we give them autonomy. I am very sorry indeed, if we are going to proceed as a parliament next year to organize those large territories into one or more provinces, that we shall be compelled to sit down and adjust a debt account. I think it is better to proceed along the lines we have been following in the past, giving the territories what we consider fairly and reasonably sufficient for their purposes. But by no means let us raise up a debt account against them, which will be standing in the way and perhaps be a troublesome matter to settle when we come to arrange for the political autonomy of the provinces. It will make no difference to the Dominion. We are getting no interest, and I do not suppose for a moment that when the adjustment is made even the principal will ever be asked for. If we treat the territories respectfully, treat them handsomely, and keep them in good humour, I think we will make better terms with them when we come to settle all these questions. But by no means let us do something that will only prove a vexed question hereafter. Now with regard to the other question, I have only to say that the sooner we give these provinces political autonomy the better, for then we do away with these annual grants. As at present they are regarded as wards of the Dominion, and I think the sooner we close this account by bringing about a different arrangement for the government of these provinces and doing away with these annual grants, the better for the Dominion and the better for the territories. I would advise the Finance Minister to create no debt account, because if we do anything

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: of that kijrd we may have a troublesome matter to settle when we come to erect them into provinces.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: Has the territorial government been consulted regarding this $250,000 and has it consented to its being placed in the way the hon. minister proposes ? that is by adding it to the debt and making it a matter of readjustment in connection with its account in the future.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: The correspondence on the subject was brought down some time ago. I think perhaps I would not be justified in saying that the territorial government consented. Really, it was unnecessary to ask their consent inasmuch as this is not a matter of obligation upon them at all. If the territorial government do not wish to avail themselves of the privileges of this Act they need not do so. Therefore, as we are not imposing any obligation upon them, we did not deem it necessary to obtain their consent. I think, perhaps, the territorial government would be pleased to have as large a grant as the government would give aud that they would prefer to have this in the form of a grant and not something to be charged to the debt account.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: Have they applied for this subsidy ?

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext:
No, but the territorial government for many years applied not only to this government, but to the former government asking for a larger grant. They always err on the side of liberality in asking, and I think our responses have not been less generous-m fact, they are much more generous-than they have been under our predecessors. But, having represented their needs to us, we have to some extent exercised our own discretion as to the various methods by which we could meet their needs. I do not wish to say that the territorial government have requested that this method shall be adopted, but I think the territorial government will find this arrangement useful to them. If they do not need this money it will not be pi-essed on them and no harm is done.
Mi\ SPROULE. I understood the hon. minister to specify two items in regard to which it was represented as being necessary that an expenditure should be made.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext:
As respects these two particular items they did apply some months ago and we have decided by Order in. Council that we shall X'ecom-mend parliament to make provision for these two works. We are proposing in the supplementary estimates to make that provision, not as a charge against this grant, but out of the ordinary grant for the current year. The government of the North-west Territories applied for these special appro-

priations, but they aid not ask for a general credit such as we now propose.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: I hope the hon. Minister of Finance will consider the propriety ot continuing the grant. That country is being settled far and wide. It is quite different from any other portion of Canada. Bridges have to be built. Of late years bridges have been swept away as quickly as they have been built. In view of the extraordinary circumstances prevailing there I hope the hon. Minister of Finance will consider the propriety of continuing the grant rather than of charging these advances to the debt account. This plan which he proposes may cause a misunderstanding in the future in view of the fact that there are no specified terms upon which this debt is to be created.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: We do both. First we give them a liberal grant

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: I understand perfectly.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: We are not ungenerous. We give them a grant this year, about four times as much as it was when we came into office.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: I do not say that you have been ungenerous. I do say that you are creating a debt and they must have need of the money or you would not be giving them an opportunity of borrowing it. One of the worst things connected with giving them autonomy in my opinion is that they would be free to create debts.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: My hon. friend has touched the serious objection to autonomy. Still there are different kinds of debts. When you say that the matter is to be subject to adjustment in the debt account, it does not absolutely decide on which side the debt shall be. In my province we have $1,000,000 in the debt account, but instead of being a burden on the province the Dominion has to pay interest upon it. I do not want to make any dangerous admissions as to what will be the case in regard to the North-west Territories, because, having responsibility, it devolves upon me to speak with reserve, but when the time comes to adjust the debt account it does not follow that it will be charged against the Territories.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext:
Although it may be a question as to which party the debt will be charged against there is no question about the $250,000 referred to in this resolution, because the resolution says :
All sums so advanced to the government of the Nonth-weat Territories shall be charged in an account to be known as ' The North-west Territories Debt Account,' and shall, in any financial arrangement that may be made in connection with the organization of a province or provinces in the said territories, be taken
into consideration as a debt owing by the said territories to the Dominion of Canada.
This will be owing by the territories. That is what I object to. I think we should leave them in the position in which they are now as we have been satisfying the territories very well until we are prepared to make a different arrangement with them which will not be, perhaps, beyond twelve months, according to the Minister of Finance. It would be a pity to create a debt or anything that could be called a debt because it might lead to a dispute when the settlement is being brought about. We are told that they have not been consulted about this, that they have not asked for this money and they may not ask for it. I think perhaps they may be independent enough not to ask for it, because I believe it is their right to have it and it should not have been charged to them as a debt to be held up before them one or two years hence when we come to finally arrange with them.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext: I am afraid I have not been able to make myself clear. Suppose when the adjustment of accounts takes place between the new province and the Dominion it should be found that there was-I do not like to name the amount-a million dollars to be placed at the credit of the North-west Territories in the debt account. The only difference between the situation then and now is that instead of waiting for the event and placing the money to their credit next year we are giving them the right to draw upon it in advance and it then has to be adjusted in connection with the general arrangement of the farmers of the province.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT OF THE NORTH-WEST TERRITORIES-FINANCIAL AID.
speechtext:
Does the hon. Minister of Finance expect that when they are organized into a province in that way, and when they are supposed to get a credit of $1,000,000 they will only get three-quarters of a million that it will be satisfactory to them ? I do not think it should be so. I suggest that the hon. Minister of Finance drop the matter and bring it up again when he gives them autonomy.

On clauses 1, 2 and 3-salaries of deputy heads.

Under the present Civil Service Act, the salary of a deputy head upon his appointment is $3,200. The Act says that the minimum salary of a deputy head shall be $3,200 and the maximum $4,000, but the Act does not provide any rule for increases, and so we have the anomaly of some deputy heads remaining for years at the minimum, and others more fortunate, getting the maximum salaries. It is proposed in future to apply the same rule of annual increases to deputy heads, as applies to other civil servants. At the same time, an effort is made to deal with the deputies who are at present in the service. Deputy heads newly appointed will received $3,500 with annual increases of $100 until they attain the maximum. Those now in the service are to be treated in the same manner, $100 a year being credited to them until they reach the maximum. It is proposed to treat the deputy heads in the Departments of Finance, Railways and Canals and Justice exceptionally. In the event of the Deputy Minister of Justice being at the time of his appointment a barrister of 10 years standing ; the Deputy Minister of Finance, for 10 years the manager of a bank or a brauch bank, or the Deputy of Railways and Canals, a civil engineer of at least 10 years standing, he shall be entitled to a $1,000 in addition to the amount mentioned. These three deputies shall get $4,500 at their ap-

poiutment, and attain a maximum of $5,000, instead of $4,000 as in/ the other cases. There is also a provision that the present Deputy Minister of Finance shall get the benefit of this Act without having to wait for a number of years. It would be more convenient if we dispose of the resolution clause by clause, and I therefore move the adoption of paragraphs two and three, referring to deputy heads.

On behalf of the civil service, I desire to thank the Postmaster General for having withdrawn the one sided Bill which he submitted to parliament a few weeks ago, and on my own behalf, I desire to express my thanks to him for adopting in this new Bill, the principle which I laid down in the amendment which I had the honour to submit to this House when his first Bill was presented. As the Bill is to be adopted by sections, I shall confine myself to dealing with these first clauses respecting deputy heads. Bet me say at the outset, that I believe that a gentleman who is capable of filling the position of deputy head of one of the departments of government, should not be treated on entering the service as if he were an apprentice, and be compelled to start at a minimum salary. Any man who is capable of properly filling the position of a deputy minister, ought to start at the maximum' salary of his class. I also take objection to the provision in this clause which gives an additional salary to the Deputy Ministers of Finance, Railways, and Justice. It would seem to me that no discrimination should be made in the salaries of the deputies. Each department of government is recognized as of the same importance and each minister receives the same salary, and if one minister is as important as another, then the deputies should be on the same footing. Again, the fact that a man has served 10 years as manager of a bank or a branch bank, before being appointed Deputy Minister of Finance, does not give him any particular qualification. I know managers of branch banks who are no better qualified to be a Deputy Minister of Finance, than any ordinary accountant. Then, as to the Deputy Minister of Jnstice ; there are lawyers who have been practising for ten years

cial experts for deputy ministers of other departments of government. Why not treat all alike ? I do not object that the Postmaster General should give these three deputy heads an additional $1,000, but the point I make is that their minimum salary being $4,500 and the maximum $5,000, the salaries of the other deputies should be the same. An expert business man is in every respect just as valuable as an expert professional man, and if deputy ministers who are professional gentlemen are worth the salary which it is proposed to give them, then the deputies in what might be called the commercial departments of the government, are worth the same. As the minister proposes to discuss these resolutions clause by clause, I shall not say more on this part of the resolution.

Under this Act, do I understand that a deputy minister is not required to pass a civil service examination before his appointment ? I assume that an outsider could be appointed over the head of a man who has given years of efficient service, and who would be entitled to promotion.

By the Civil Service Act any one of the age of 21 years is eligible to be apointed deputy head of most of the departments. It is not necessary for any one to pass an examination for such a position. There are many other offices high up in the service to which men can be appointed without passing a civil service examination.
I wanted to know whether a person had to pass a civil service examination in order to be qualified for the position of deputy minister ?
No.

In that case an officer who had served a number of years in a department and was familiar with the work of the department and entitled by seniority to the position of deputy head, might be passed over and an outsider might be appointed over his head so that he would be deprived of the promotion to which he would rightly be entitled. I suppose, therefore, that the position of deputy heads of departments are merely political appointments.

We have made no change in the law. If the hon. gentleman will examine the lists of deputy heads appointed from time to time by various governments he will find constantly recurring cases of persons who were not in the service being appointed deputy heads.

This measure, whichl I think is timely and justified, will be well received by the public gener-1 ally, and will be thankfully acknowledged by the civil service. It is true that in a measure as regards both the deputy ministers and the other classes of civil servants it does not grant exactly what the civil service expected and it does not grant all that I for one have urged the government to grant, but I believe generally it is a substantial measure of justice and that it will be thankfully received by the civil servants. So far as I am concerned it has my cordial and thankful support. It is quite in consonance with the traditions of the Liberal party in the treatment of the
civil service ; it is not quite as generous a measure as, that which was proposed by the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) in 1S75 when he was a member of the Mackenzie administration, but it is in many respects an improvement on the civil service law which has been on the statute-book for many many years. Then, too, under the Mackenzie administration, the civil service received what it never received under any other government, it was granted bonuses for very large sums. In 1874 a bonus of $75,000 was paid by the Mackenzie government to the civil service which amounted to a 15 per cent increase on the salaries then paid. A bonus of a similar amount was paid in 1875 and a third one, which was paid some years afterwards, amounted to $30,000. The Bill is timely and justified because the civil service to-day has very much increased labours. It has to be in many respects more proficient and its members have to give more time to the performance of their work, in addition to which the work of the civil servants is of more importance than it was formerly. The growth of our country in the last few years has not only increased the work of the civil service but has brought it into contact with the civil service and with the officers of state in other countries.
I wish it tb be understood that if you are going to allow the hon. member (Mr. Belcourt) to speak generally on the Bill the same rule should be applied to all the other members of the committee.

I understood that the committee decided to take this Bill up clause by clause and I understand that the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) is speaking to the first clause ; I hope he will confine himself closely to the first clause.
I do not object to him speaking, but I want to have the same right.

It seems to me it would be more convenient if we were not confined to any particular clause, because it is necessary to travel over the whole Civil Service Act. It would be much more convenient to allow a general discussion on it so as to avoid the necessity of going over and over it again.
Would the hon. gentleman excuse me ?

Then, I prefer not to give way to him.
I was confined to the first section, and why should not other hon. gentlemen be equally restricted ?
As there seems to be a desire to discuss the whole subject generally, I suggest that we should consider the whole question before going into it clause by clause.

I was just about to say that on account of the growth of the country and its increasing importance and its expansion in all branches of the affairs of state, our civil service has not only been given increased work, but has been brought into contact with the civil service of other countries, which has added to its efficiency. It may be said that the members of out-civil service, who have been called on to deal with the civil service of our countries, have acquitted themselves in a very creditable manner, but the result is that larger money demands have been made upon them and they have to fill positions in society which compel them to incur extra expenditure. Speaking generally, it may be said with truth that the civil service of Canada is composed of faithful, loyal, honourable and efficient men. In order to show how very much things have changed in Canada, let me draw a comparison between the conditions now and those which existed at the time of confederation. At the time of confederation our population was 3,500,000; it is now 5,500,000. Our revenue, which was then $14,000,000, has increased to $53,000,000. Our expenditure has risen from $14,000,000 then to $50,000,000 now. I find that in 1873, which is the earliest year for which we have returns regarding Dominion lands, the extent of Dominion lands we dealt with was 156,000 acres, whereas in 1902 the amount was 3,750,000 acres. The post offices opened in Canada at the time of confederation numbered 3,600; last year they numbered 10,000. The number of letters carried have increased from 18,000,000 at confederation to 240,000,000 last year. Our post office revenue, which was $1,024,000 at confederation, has increased to $5,250,000 last year. Our imports and exports amounted to $130,000,000 at confederation. In 1902 they aggregated $430,000,000. Our public assets increased from $20,000,000 to $100,000,000. At confederation we had 2,200 miles of railway; to-day we have 20,000. Our government expenditure has increased from $500,000 at confederation to $8,000,000. Our expenditure on railways and canals, which was then $130,000, is to-day $2,500,000. On public works, from the modest sum of $200,000 spent at confederation, we have reached $4,500,000 to-day. The number of our post office savings banks has increased from 81 to 915, and our deposits in those banks from $200,000 to $43,000,000. Our first shipments of grain, of which we have any record, amounted to 500 bushels in 1896. Last year they amounted to from 120,000,000 to 150,000,000 bushels.

Up to 1882 there was no attempt to deal with the salaries of the civil service, except in 1875, when a Bill was introduced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and discussed in the House, but did not go beyond its second reading. What are the messengers paid ?

The messengers are paid a daily allowance which varies very much. The smallest annual increase in England is $75. In view of these figures-which I may say I have known for a long time-I have nearly every year since I have had the honour of a seat in this- House, deemed it my duty, not only as representing a large number of civil servants but as a citizen, to draw the attention of the government to the fact that our civil service is underpaid, and that it should receive better treatment. I have from time to time submitted to the government by memorials and otherwise suggestions in that regard, and if you will bear with me I would like to give a general outline of what those suggestions have been. I do not hope that they will or can be adopted, but I think I will give my suggestions to the House, commending them to the impartial and kindly consideration of every member of the committee, feeling confident as I do that it is the desire of every one to see full justice done to the civil service. Most every one must realize that it is in the interests of the community at large and in the interest of the better administration of our affairs that the civil servants should be properly treated.
Now dealing with the deputy heads I had thought that the provision which has been made applicable to a certain number, for instance to the Deputy Minister of Justice, the Deputy Minister of Finance and the Deputy Minister of Railways ^nd Canals, might also be applied to the other deputies, and that after ten years service a deputy head should receive $1,000 in addition to the maximum fixed by the new Bill. I will not deal with this at great length, and I only make the suggestion believing that it is one which is justified by the reasons I have mentioned, namely, the cost of living and the tremendous duties and responsibilities which are cast upon the deputy heads of departments. Dealing with the service generally outside of the deputy heads, my suggestions were these-and I may say at once that they are taken, with one single exception, from the Bill which was introduced into this House in 1875 by the present Mr. BELCOURT.
Minister of Trade and Commerce. The figures which I have suggested are also those which the civil servants themselves, after considering the matter many times, have submitted to the government. First, for grade A, $2,400 to $2,SOO. This has been adopted in the present Bill. Chief clerks were to be $2,000 to $2,400. The present Bill provides for paying them $1,900 to $2,500. I had suggested that first-class clerks should receive $1,600 and a maximum of $2,000, with an annual increase of $100 instead of $50 ; that second-class senior clerks should receive $1,200 to $1,600 with an annual increase of $50; second-class juniors, $800 to $1,100 with an annual increase of $50 ; third-class clerks, $500 to $750, with an annual increase of $50 ; temporary or permanent messengers, sorters or packers, stenographers and typewriters, $500 to $750, also with annual increases of $50. I had also suggested that a new class of messengers might be created. The messengers in the different departments, as I understand, are all on an equal footing, they are all receiving the same salary. None of them, as I understand, has any particular authority over the others. I had thought that for the better administration of the departments it would be well to have a new class of messengers created, to be called chief messengers, and I had suggested that in that case, there being only one for each department, he should receive a maximum or $750, with an annual increase of $50. I had also suggested that writers and clerks, packers, sorters, messengers, stenographers and typewriters might be promoted to the third-class or to the second junior class. I understand that these members of the service were eligible to the junior seeoud class, but were not so to the third class. The Postmaster General has adopted that suggestion, and by section 14 of the resolutions, the gentlemen who have been performing that duty are mow eligible to the third class.
It is well known to those who have had occasion to deal with the different departments that there are a number of messengers, packers and sorters who have been for a number of years, some of them as long as 15 or 20 years, doing really clerical work, and who are still messengers, packers or sorters, whom it was very difficult indeed to promote to junior second-class clerkships on account of the great disparity of salaries received by messengers and junior second-class clerks. That provision, as I say, has been adopted and made part of these resolutions. I had also suggested that temporary officers employed in various branches of the departments as technical officers might be put on the permanent list. It is known that there are gentlemen in the service who have been there, some for 10 and others as long as 35 years, and who have always been and are still on the temporary list, men who

are in receipt of salaries as high as $2,800. It always seemed to me to be an anomaly that men should he in the civil service for a great number of years, and yet be only temporary. They are deprived of the benefits of superannuation, their appointment is very precarious, and it has to be renewed by Order in Council every six months. It seemed to me to be an anomaly that men should be, to use an expression we heard not long ago employed by the Minister of Finance ' permanent temporaries.' It seemed to me proper that these clerks, who are in the service to stay and who will stay there as long as they do not resign, should be put on the permanent list. I think it would add considerably to the independence of the civil service, and relieve the service from the necessity of resorting to political pull, and log rolling, and a lot of other undesirable things to secure promotion. I hope that at some future time when this Bill is under revision, the government will deem it proper to adopt my suggestion and to make all these persons permanent. My suggestion was that they should he placed in a class the salary of which corresponds with the salary they are now getting. If a man is in receipt of a salary of $1,200, he might be put in the class of second clerks ; if he is in receipt of a salary of $2,000 he might be put in the class of chief clerks, and so on. My suggestion did not mean any increase of salary, it did not mean an increase of expenditure at all ; it simply meant that these temporary clerks who have, as I say, been there for so many years, should be put on the permanent list at the salary they "were then receiving. These are the suggestions which I have from time to time submitted to the government, suggestions which, again, I say, I commend to the kindly consideration of the committee. I need not remind the committee, as it is known to everybody, that since confederation the cost of living in the most essential necessities of life has tremendously increased, I think I am quite within the mark when I say that the increased cost of living since confederation is at least between 30 and 40 per cent, and that that increase in the cost of living has taken place very largely during the last five or six years. The suggestions which I had the honour to submit would have involved an increase in the salaries of the civil service to the extent of 15 per cent over the present salaries. I have made a computation of what the increases that are provided for by the present Bill amount to. The increases above the present salaries of the civil service which are proposed by this legislation are as follows :-Deputy ministers, 25 per cent ; chief clerks (old class), 41 per cent ; first class clerks, 54 per cent ; second class clerks, 7i per cent ; junior second class, 10 per cent. If we leave out the deputy heads we find that the average increase of all classes of clerks is 6i per cent. The suggestion that I made would have provided for an increase of 15 per cent and I think that such an increase is justified when the fact is known that there has been an increase in the cost of living of at least 30 per cent. The government, I think, might very properly have provided for an increase in the salaries of the civil service of 15 per cent. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright). He dexterously handed the paper to the Clerk of the House and the thing was done. I have already expressed the hope on another occasion, that the leader of the opposition in this House should also receive the recognition which he deserves. The leader ofi the opposition-and I could not mention it at any more appropriate time because he is not present and because of the great length of this session-has been in constant attendance^ upon his duties during this long session which has dragged its length for more than half a year. It is plain to every one in this House that the present leader of the opposition, who has a very large and lucrative practice, has had to sacrifice his profession and his time and we regret very much that he has had in a measure to sacri-Mr. BELCOURT.
lice his health. It seems to me that under these circumstances the leader of the opposition has very strong claims upon the consideration of the House and I think some adequate provision should be made for him when this matter is under consideration. I have another suggestion and it is this. It is known that there are in this country still living quite a number of gentlemen who have served thieir country faithfully and well for a number of years in the position of ministers of the Crown. Some of them have given a quarter, and in some instances, half their lifetime to the public service. They have given the best of their years and of their talent to the country's service, and unfortunately some of them have left office in almost destitute circumstances. The country owes it to these men to make provisions so that they may pass the remainder of their days at least removed from want. I believe that this suggestion will commend itself to parliament. It is on the line of the principle adopted in the case of others of our public servants, and I hope that the government will consider it favourably. I realize that it is not in my power to amend the Bill in the direction I have suggested, because under our constitution no private member has a right to amend a money Bill so that it will increase the charges upon the revenue of the country. However, Sir, I offer these suggestions, and I trust that they may receive the early and earnest consideration of the government. Before I resume my seat, on behalf of the civil service, I again give my hearty thanks to the government for the substantial measure of justice that this proposal accords.

The hon. the senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt) says that during the seven years he has been a member of this House he has been able to induce the present government to increase the salaries of the civil service by six per cent. I did not say that 6 per cent was the extent of the increase, I said six and three quarters per cent it is not all that I suggested, passed and hoped for. But that is six and three quarters per cent better than all the governments supported by

my hon. friend ever did for the civil servants, it is that much better than was done by their predecessors. It is well known amongst the civil servants that the preceding governments, particularly when Mr. Foster was Minister of Finance, did everything that they could to bring the civil service into contempt in the country. It degraded the civil servants, so much so that when this government came into power they found it impossible to mete out the measure of justice which the civil service was entitled to. From confederation down to 1896, while the party which my hon. friend supports was in power, the salaries of the civil servants had not increased. Not one single attempt was made to l'aise the salaries of the civil servants notwithstanding the fact that the cost of living in Canada had materially increased, and notwithstanding the fact that the labours of the civil servants had materially increased. On the contrary, whatever privileges the civil servants had enjoyed previously under the Liberal government of 1875 were taken away. It was the Liberal government of 1875 which granted a bonus to the civil servants and which granted bonuses in the two years following. It was the Liberal government that gave the franking privilege to the service, which Mr. Foster took the first opportunity of withdrawing from the service after he came into office. My efforts on behalf of the civil servants during the past seven years and which have been constant, not so much in this House as outside of it, have, I know, resulted in bringing about the results which I have stated and which will be in a large measure embodied in the Bill based upon the present resolutions.

entitled to be called the senior member than the hon. gentleman who claims that distinction. However, that is not the point that I rose to make reference to. is no precedent for a whole class of officers being transferred by Act of parliament to the permanent list It must be that they can be appointed and removed by the Governor in Council as other civil servants are, with the exception of the judiciary. Suppose I had one of these officers in the Post Office Department, and I desired to have him appointed to a clerkship, it would be necessary first to create that additional clerkship under the Act, and then parliament would have to vote the money for his salary. These two things being done, it would be open to the Governor in Council to transfer that officer from the temporary to the permanent class. It does happen that there are men in the service performing responsible duties, and some of them an receipt of large salaries, and yet they are temporary in the eye of the law. I received a memorial from a number of gentlemen in the Interior Department asking to be transferred to the permanent list. To do that, each case would have to be considered to a certain extent in the same way as if it were a case of promotion, and if the Minister of the Interior happened to be in Canada at the time, perhaps he would have seen his way to ask for additional clerks, and make it possible to appoint these gentleman. as 1 have said because some classes either on the inside or the outside service are not dealt with it does not follow that their ' cases will not in due time come up. Last year, for example, parliament was good enough to pass a measure on my advice increasing the salaries of certain classes in the outside service in my own department. Speaking from memory, the classes (affected were composed of messengers, porters and packers, men in my department who make up parcels of supplies, &c., to be sent to different postmasters throughout the country and to do similar work. I found these men with a maximum salary of $500 and last year parliament passed a Bill increasing that maximum to $600. I felt then and I feel now, that in making increases the most urgent cases are those of the people who receive the lower salaries. By this measure the class of messengers, packers and porters, to which I have referred, will be in receipt of a maximum salary of $700 as against $500 when we took office, an increase of 20 per cent. That increase, I know, receives the hearty approval of hon. members on both sides of the House. With reference to the class of temporary technical officers to whom reference has been made, I suppose that if the various ministers could direct their attention to the whole matter and go through a regular course of house cleaning and say which of these should be transferred to the permanent list they could be appointed in the regular way by the creation of additional clerkships. it is not because we do not wish to have them increased. The fact is, without wishing to make any point about it, but to be perfectly frank, that there is some truth in the statement that formerly, before the change of government, the civil service had been the subject of criticism and talk, and I think parliament did a rather unwise thing in abolishing the third-class clerkships in the inside service. That class went up to $1,000 and represented a very large proportion of the civil service and it is there that you have to be even more considerate than with the higher classes. A certain amount of public opinion was developed against the civil service which was referred to even in campaigns as we have all seen, and many people in criticising the service alluded perhaps unkindly to the civil service. From my few years in government I can say, speaking with reference to the officers of my department-and I now speak of it as of them as I would speak of employees in private life, and as I would wish to be spoken of-I say there is in my department without any question as good, efficient and loyal a staff as any country could desire and many of the employees in that department are men who are I consider wasting their lives in the public service, because the prizes in the public service are not such as should command the ability and fidelity possessed by many of these men, and I think that the civil service of Canada generally is not properly remunerated. It has been suggested that the increases should be permitted automatically and that the civil servants should get their increases as a matter or right. This has never been the unvarying practice ; the practice has always been that the increase is voted by parliament as apportioned by the government. After we took office, for a time, these increases were suspended and that was no doubt prompted by the feeling created in the public mind and in our own mind that the service required overhauling and we could not then permit increase to occur automatically as now, when we are more familiar with the service practically do, for we feel now that this automatic increase can be made without any injustice to the service and to the country.

Will the members of the outside service, in the inland revenue and customs departments throughout the country receive the same treatment as these servants for whom you are providing under this resolution ?

cial Bill dealing with the outside service of the Post Office Department was passed. Mr. ItEID (Grenville). I do not wish to detain the House any longer, but the hon. minister did not quite understand the point I was trying to make.

I think I owe an apology to the hon. gentleman from Ottawa who gives the government his confidence. It is quite correct-and I am not saying this for the purpose of making any capital or robbing any one of capital ; we are glad in legislation of this kind to have the concurrence of all classes of representatives-but it has been said that any member representing Ottawa and supporting the government is naturally the intermediary through whom the civil service seek to reach the government and the House- that my hon. friend (Mr. Belcourt) in the discharge of his duty, and he could not have done less, brought this matter to the attention of the government and to my attention as a member of the government. My sympathies, went out first of all towards the lower paid grades and for this reason, although I had taken pretty ample notes, yet I had not been as impressed in regard to the agreements on behalf of the higher classes as perhaps I should have been. But the cases that made the greatest impression on me were the classes I have spoken of, the temporary writers and clerks, messengers, packers, etc., men who came in at $400 with an annual increase of $30 per year until $600 was reached, and there they stopped. There is a class that begins at $300-sorters, messengers and porters-and who went up to $500. There is a very large number of those. In my department they are particularly strong. I dare say these various classes number up to the best part of a hundred. I felt I was really reaching most of the cases in dealing with these classes, and therefore in the first Bill I gave particular attention to them by establishing a third class, with a maximum pay of $700. There was provision in the first Bill, as there is in the present, for all that class being transferred from the status of temporary clerks and writers and so on, to third class. There was provision in the first Bill for the temporary class and writers- I do not know that it went as far as the packers-but there is in this Bill, and all of that class eligible for transfer may be transferred. I felt it my duty to half apologize to my hon. friend when I introduced the first Bill, because I knew I had not gone as far as he desired. I rather innocently explained that I had not gone as far as he diesired. I could not make that announcement privately, and it was my duty, in justice to him, to make it to the House on account of the especial responsibility which devolves on him as the representative of the city supporting the government. This is just how this second resolution came in, if you want a confession. As soon as my Bill was introduced, my hon. friend remonstrated with me. He said that I was not a strong enough supporter of his measure, and he appealed to the Premier. He took the memorial of the civil service, which had been prepared some time before-I am not quarrelling with him about it-but he passed by me and presented it to the Premier. I happened to be away at the time, and when I came back I received an intimation from the Premier that the measure was to be introduced in its present shape. I am extremely glad that my hon. friend on the other side has furthered my effort by presenting his resolution. Neither party need try to make political capital out of this matter. Both this side and the opposition owe a duty to the civil service. Let us do our duty fairly to a deserving class, and not try to win favours except on our merits. If I tried to point out shortcomings of the previous government I might succeed, but what good would come of all that ? If you pass the resolution I shall leave it in committee until to-morrow, in case any hon. gentleman desires to make any further remarks.

I wish to say a few words on this subject, and there is no more appropriate time than now. In the first place, I desire to say a word as to the speech of the hon. senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Belcourt). If that hon. gentleman had really desired to do justice to the civil service he would have welcomed assistance from any source instead of abusing the hon. junior member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett) for trying to get the increase of salary the hon. senior member said he was trying to secure. I do not think the service will give him much credit. In the course of his remarks he said that the Conservative party had been in power for eighteen years and had done nothing for the civil service. Is that true ? Does he forget the first Civil Service Act which put the civil service upon a non-political basis ? That was passed by the Conservative party in 1882. Before that, the service was a rather heterogeneous class employed largely on political lines. It provided that, certain examinations should be passed, so that, whether a man belonged to one party or the other on .passing the examination he was eligible for the civil service. In my own riding I had a prominent Reformer appointed entirely upon his merits, because he was recommended as a graduate of Toronto University, and capable of taking the position that was vacant, [DOT]and because the man whom I had had in view was reported to me as not suitable. I took this man, who was a Reformer and whose family were Reformers, and got him appointed. There was no question as to which party he belonged to, but simply as to his qualifications ; and he proved that he had the qualifications for the position and therefore got it. By this Civil Service

Act the service was put upon a business and non-political basis. The principle of promotion according to ability and qualification was established. And, in addition to that they were given statutory increases, if they were faithful and efficient officers and were recommended by the deputy head. I admit that, what the Postmaster General says is true. If my amendment is out of order, I. do not wish to press it any further.

I think any movement of this kind at this late date of the session would imperil this measure. Public business, even of a very urgent character, towards the close of a session is often deferred, and my hon. friend 1 am sure does not want to imperil this Bill. It has made some progress. It will take time to draft new amendments and get the assent of the Crown. Then we have the second chamber to deal with. If my hon. friend is desirous to have some benefit given to the civil service, he will not interpose any measure that involves delay.
Certainly not.

I wish to amend section 5 :
The minimum salary of a chief clerk shall be $1,900 per annum, and the maximum salary shall be $2,500 per annum.
I wish to amend that so that it shall read :
The minimum salary of a chief clerk shall be $1,900 per annum, with an annual increase of $50 up to a maximum of $2,500 per annum.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
Progress reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will we take up to-morrow ?
The Redistribution Bill.
And if we should dispose of that early in the day, what then ?
Have you that in anticipation?
We will allow the Iron, gentleman to sleep under that impression, anyway.
I suppose the Transcontinental Railway Bill, but of that I am not quite certain.
You would not have it printed.
Well, we will have to find something else in order to keep the House busy. We may proceed with the motion of my hon. friend the Postmaster General.

May I ask the hon. Minister of Finance when the supplementary Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
estimates and the railway resolutions will be brought down ? The hon. gentleman promised them this week, and we are getting pretty near the end of the week now.
The deck has been pretty well cleared of othqr questions, and I would hope that early next week both of these matters will be before the House.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 1.40 a.m. Friday.
Friday, September 25, 1903.
